sections.skill: Describe AI as a broad term for systems that do thinking-like tasks

questions.domain: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
questions.prompt: Which description fits this course's meaning of AI?

choices.text: Any computer program at all, including a basic pocket calculator
A single website that answers questions in a chat window
One specific robot that thinks in exactly the same way as a person
A broad name for computer systems that do tasks linked with human thinking

questions.correct_answer: A broad name for computer systems that do tasks linked with human thinking
questions.intro: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) is a broad name for computer systems that do tasks we usually connect with human thinking, such as recognizing speech, sorting photos, predicting what comes next, recommending a song, or writing a paragraph. It is an umbrella term, not one machine: a spam filter, a map app's travel-time estimate and a chatbot can all be called AI, yet they work differently and do different jobs. Calling something "AI" does not tell you how well it works or what it can do. To understand a tool, ask what task it performs, what it takes in, and what it gives back.
questions.feedback: AI is an umbrella term for many kinds of systems that do thinking-like tasks.

sections.skill: See "AI" as a broad label, like the word "vehicle"

questions.domain: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
questions.prompt: Why is "vehicle" a good comparison for "AI" in the passage?

choices.text: Both words describe ways of moving people around
Both words describe one machine with many parts
Both words name a broad group of different things
Both words describe machines that have engines

questions.correct_answer: Both words name a broad group of different things
questions.intro: Think of the word VEHICLE. A bicycle, a bus and a cargo ship are all vehicles, but you would not expect a bicycle to cross an ocean. "Vehicle" names a broad group, not one machine, and knowing that something is a vehicle tells you little about its speed or range. "AI" works the same way. It names a broad group of computer systems that do tasks such as recognizing, predicting, recommending or generating. Knowing that something is "AI" tells you little about what it can do. You learn more by asking what job it does.
questions.feedback: Each word covers many different things that work differently.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Look past an "AI" label when a decision matters

questions.domain: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
questions.prompt: A budgeting app calls itself "AI-powered," but it only applies one fixed rule: save 10 percent of each deposit. What is the best conclusion?

choices.text: It is more reliable because it says "AI-powered"
The label may be marketing; a fixed rule is doing the work
It must be learning from millions of other users' data
It cannot work, since it is not "real" AI

questions.correct_answer: The label may be marketing; a fixed rule is doing the work
questions.intro: Because "AI" is a broad label, it is used loosely. Marketers may call a simple fixed rule "AI" to sound modern, and some tools that do use learned patterns never mention AI at all. Two products both described as "AI-powered" can differ greatly in quality, cost and risk. When a claim matters, for example when a school, employer or bank says AI helps make a decision, look past the label: ask what the system does, what information it uses, how it was tested, and who checks its results. A label is a starting point for questions, not an answer.
questions.feedback: Labels are used loosely; look at what the system actually does.
